title: Voters Worry About Election Integrity | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: A Gallup poll of 23,000+ voters taken April 24–June 10, 2026 finds cross-partisan majorities doubting the November midterms will be free and fair, with 67 percent fearing political leaders will pressure election officials to change outcomes. Alongside that, Lindsay tracks Trump's net approval falling to -20.6, a 6.4-point Democratic generic-ballot lead, $4.10 gas eroding Republican support for the Iran campaign, and a Republican caucus that will emerge more MAGA regardless of who wins.

insights.claim: A Gallup survey of more than 23,000 voters conducted April 24 through June 10, 2026 found 67 percent expressing a great deal or a fair amount of concern that political leaders will pressure election officials to change election outcomes — the top-ranked threat of six tested.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: Widespread expectation of a contested result raises the odds of a post-election legal and street-level standoff that markets typically price as a volatility event, not a policy event.
insights.quote: The threat that topped the list for Americans, with 67 percent expressing “a great deal” or “a fair amount” of concern, is that political leaders will pressure election officials to change election outcomes.
insights.locator: The threat that topped the list

insights.claim: Concern about the November U.S. midterms runs deep across the whole ballot-integrity stack: 57 percent worry ballots will not be properly handled, counted, or secured, 52 percent worry about voter intimidation near polling places, and 50 percent worry their own ballots will not be counted.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: Half the electorate doubting their own vote counts is a precondition for post-election legitimacy fights; watch state-level litigation filings as the leading indicator.

insights.claim: Distrust of the 2026 U.S. election process is not a partisan artifact: at least 40 percent of the public is concerned about each of the six aspects Gallup asked about, and a majority had concerns about four of them.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: Because doubt is cross-partisan, neither party has an incentive to de-escalate integrity rhetoric — the tail risk of a disputed outcome is systemic, not one-sided.
insights.quote: While the partisan differences are notable, they should not obscure the fact that Americans across the political spectrum worry about election integrity.
insights.locator: While the partisan differences are notable

insights.claim: Republicans and Democrats fear mirror-image failure modes of the same election: Republicans worry most that ballots will not be properly handled, counted, or secured and least about voter intimidation, while Democrats and Independents worry most about political pressure to change outcomes and least about their votes not being counted.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: The two camps will contest different parts of the process, meaning a close result invites simultaneous challenges on incompatible grounds and a longer resolution timeline.
insights.locator: As the table shows, Republicans, Democrats

insights.claim: The absence of any historical polling baseline on election integrity is itself evidence the issue is new: pollsters generally do not ask questions about issues that are not on the public's mind, so until recently election integrity was not a significant policy issue.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: A brand-new concern with no baseline can move fast in either direction — treat current levels as unanchored rather than as a stable regime.
insights.quote: Pollsters generally do not ask questions about issues that are not on the public’s mind.
insights.locator: How do these numbers look from a historical perspective?

insights.claim: The polling window closed before Trump's July 16 nationally televised address alleging foreign interference in past U.S. elections, so the measured 67 percent concern level predates that catalyst and likely understates current anxiety.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: Expect the next integrity poll to print higher; the current numbers are a floor, not a peak.
insights.locator: The poll was conducted from April 24

themes.theme: Trump approval and the generic ballot

insights.claim: Trump's June approval uptick reversed in July: an average of national polls has 38.2 percent approving versus 39.3 percent on July 3, with 58.8 percent disapproving, putting net approval at -20.6 points, the lowest of his second term.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: A second-term-low approval print constrains the administration's room for unpopular escalation and raises the political cost of the Iran campaign.
insights.locator: The slight uptick in Trump’s approval ratings

insights.claim: Democrats hold a 6.4-point generic-congressional-ballot lead in an average of national polls, up marginally from 6.2 a month ago but below their 2026 high of 7.1 points — a stable rather than accelerating advantage.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: A flat lead well short of prior highs argues against pricing a decisive blue wave; the range has been narrow all year.

themes.theme: Iran war, gas prices, and Republican cohesion

insights.claim: Republican approval of Trump's handling of the Iran war collapsed from 71 percent in the June AP-NORC poll to 61 percent in the late-July poll, while 96 percent of Democrats disapproved and only one in three Americans overall thinks the war has been worthwhile.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: A 10-point drop inside the base within one month is the sharpest political signal in the data — sustained escalation now costs the administration its own voters.
insights.quote: In the June AP-NORC poll, 71 percent Republicans had approved of Trump’s handling of the war.
insights.locator: The resumption of attacks on Iran

insights.claim: Gasoline at $4.10 a gallon — down from a roughly $4.50 peak earlier this year but up $0.26 month over month — is the transmission channel converting the Iran conflict into domestic political erosion for Republicans.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: Retail gasoline is the real-time gauge of the administration's tolerance for Middle East escalation heading into November; renewed upside in crude tightens that constraint.
insights.quote: Rising gas prices are likely eroding Republican approval for Operation Epic Fury.
insights.locator: Rising gas prices are likely eroding

themes.theme: Seat math and a more MAGA Congress

insights.claim: Larry Sabato's Crystal Ball now rates twenty House seats as toss-ups, up from thirteen in April, with fifteen of the twenty Republican-held — the increase driven largely by seats sliding out of the 'leans Republican' column.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: The direction of reclassification — Republican-leaning seats becoming competitive — matters more than the count for handicapping House control.
insights.locator: The latest projection by Larry Sabato’s Crystal Ball

insights.claim: The Senate map is a genuine coin flip: Crystal Ball rates Alaska, Maine, Michigan, and Ohio as toss-ups with forty-seven seats blue and forty-nine red, leaving both parties a path to the majority.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: Divided-government odds remain high, capping expectations for major legislative shifts in 2027 regardless of the House outcome.
insights.locator: On the Senate side, the Crystal Ball rates four Senate seats

insights.claim: Fifteen percent of all congressional seats are already guaranteed to change hands — thirteen senators and sixty-five representatives have declined to run or lost primaries — with eighteen states still to hold primaries.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: Unusually high turnover means committee chairs and staff relationships reset in January, degrading the predictive value of current legislative whip counts.
insights.locator: As of today, thirteen senators and sixty-five representatives

insights.claim: The Republican caucuses in both chambers will be more MAGA after November regardless of whether Republicans keep the majority, because Trump-crosswise members retired (Mitch McConnell, Thom Tillis) or lost primaries to Trump-backed challengers (Bill Cassidy, John Cornyn, Thomas Massie).
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: Even a Democratic wave will not produce a Republican pivot away from Trump, so bets on congressional checks emerging from the GOP side should be faded.
insights.quote: That suggests that congressional Republicans will not be quick to abandon Trump should a blue wave materialize in November.

themes.theme: Contrarian reads on the Democratic advantage

insights.claim: The Democratic brand remains a liability that offsets Trump's weak approval: a recent Quinnipiac poll puts approval of congressional Democrats at just 23 percent, giving Republicans material for a 'hate election' strategy.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: Betting markets keying off Trump's -20.6 net approval may be underpricing Republican resilience; the comparison set is two unpopular brands, not one.
insights.quote: Voters have to hate the Dems more than they hate us. And we have material to work with.
insights.locator: One thing Republicans have going for them

insights.claim: There is a live legal debate over whether the president can deploy the U.S. military to police domestic elections, with Lawfare analysts concluding existing law significantly limits it but that legal uncertainty invites a deploy-first, litigate-later approach.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: A domestic troop deployment around Election Day is a discrete tail risk that would hit risk assets and the dollar's institutional premium simultaneously.
insights.quote: a president with a propensity for pushing the limits of executive authority… might be tempted to capitalize on the [legal] uncertainty by sending in the troops first and letting legal challenges follow.
insights.locator: Lawfare’s Natalie K. Orpett, Molly Roberts, and Loren Voss
